USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current tariff posture on $250B of Chinese goods but do NOT escalate to the remaining $300B. Pursue structured negotiations with concrete enforcement mechanisms while keeping Huawei on the Entity List as leverage. The G20 truce is fragile — pushing further risks economic blowback with no guarantee of Chinese concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.25 reflects a dispute that has moved past neutral but has not yet reached a level materially threatening US interests. On the cost side, tariffs have raised $20.8B in revenue but the farmer bailout alone costs $28B — a net fiscal loss (NYT, July 15 2019). Harvard Business School research shows US importers are bearing nearly the full tariff incidence, with Chinese exporters refusing to cut prices (Cavallo et al., June 26 2019). Soybean exports to China are down 81%. The Fed has signaled rate cuts partly in response to trade uncertainty, and the IMF cut global growth forecasts to 2009-crisis levels. US manufacturers are relocating supply chains to Vietnam and other Asian countries, not back to the US (Salon, July 16 2019).

However, the threat is mitigated by several factors: (1) the US economy remains fundamentally strong and can absorb current tariff levels; (2) the Fed stands ready to cut rates as a buffer; (3) the tariff pressure IS extracting real pain from China — their growth has slowed to near-30-year lows; (4) the Huawei Entity List is a powerful chip that China desperately wants resolved. The US still holds leverage.

The action_score of -0.15 (slightly escalatory, within negotiate band) reflects the view that holding current pressure is justified — the $250B tariff wall and Huawei restrictions should not be rolled back without concrete Chinese concessions. But further escalation to the $300B tranche would be counterproductive: Fitch estimates it would shave 0.4% from global output, the costs would fall disproportionately on US consumers, and the political optics of tariff revenue failing to cover farmer bailouts would erode domestic support. China's failure to deliver farm purchases it promised at G20 (NYT, July 10 2019) shows Beijing is not negotiating in good faith — but the solution is patient pressure, not a tariff spiral.
key_factors: Tariff revenue ($20.8B) falls short of farmer bailout costs ($28B) — net fiscal drag
US importers bear nearly full tariff incidence; Chinese exporters not cutting prices
Soybean exports to China down 81%; agriculture sector under severe stress
Huawei Entity List remains powerful leverage — Commerce still enforcing 'presumption of denial'
China has not delivered farm purchases promised at G20 — good faith gap in negotiations
Fed signaling rate cuts as insurance against trade-war slowdown
Supply chains relocating to Vietnam/Asia, not reshoring to US
IMF cut global growth forecast to 2009 levels; JPMorgan global manufacturing index at 2012 low

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump's tariffs on Chinese imports raised $20.8 billion through Wednesday... Mr. Trump has already committed to paying American farmers hurt by the trade war $28 billion.
US importers are bearing most of the tariff increase. The pre-tariff import price of a Chinese item with a 10 percent levy only fell by 0.6 percent even 10 months after the trade war began.
Soybean exports to all countries fell to about $14.1 billion from July 2018 to April 2019, down 27 percent... Exports to China alone were down 81 percent.
G20 Osaka: Trump and Xi agree to resume talks. Existing tariffs remain; no new tariffs 'for the time being.' Trump says he will ease some Huawei restrictions (Huawei remains on the Entity List).
China has denied making any explicit commitment to buy American farm products during those discussions and instead saw large-scale purchases as contingent on progress toward a final trade deal.
The International Monetary Fund in April cut its forecast for global growth this year to 3.3%... In May, the JPMorgan global manufacturing index slumped to its lowest level since 2012.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue negotiations with the US while holding firm on core interests. Do not make new purchase commitments until the US offers concrete tariff relief. Use the post-G20 truce window to push for a structured deal that includes rollback of existing tariffs as a precondition for further concessions. Maintain the credible threat of rare earths restrictions and the unreliable entity list as leverage, but do not deploy them yet — escalation from this position would deepen economic pain without guaranteed strategic gain.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: China faces significant but not yet existential economic pressure from the trade war. GDP growth slowed to 6.2% in Q2 2019 — a 27-year low (CNN, July 15, 2019). Exports fell 1.3% in H1, with exports to the US specifically down 8.1%. Factory employment is declining at the fastest pace since the 2008 crisis. The Huawei Entity List placement (May 16) directly threatens China's tech ambitions — Google suspended Android access, major US chip suppliers paused sales, and 1,200+ companies could be affected (WSWS, May 30). The US still has a credible threat of tariffs on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese imports.

However, China retains meaningful leverage. The rare earths card is potent — China controls 90%+ of global rare earth exports, essential for US electronics, semiconductors, and military equipment (SCMP, May 29). Xi's visit to a rare earth facility in Jiangxi on May 20 was a deliberate signal. The unreliable entity list (announced May 31) gives China a mirror tool to the US Entity List. Retaliatory tariffs on ~$60B of US goods are already in place. The US side also faces costs — UBS estimates 25% tariffs on all Chinese imports would shave a full percentage point off US growth (Detroit News, June 6), and Trump faces 2020 election pressure.

The G20 Osaka truce (June 29) showed both sides recognize mutual costs of escalation. But the truce is fragile: Trump has publicly complained that China has not followed through on agricultural purchases, while China's position is that no such commitment was made independently of a broader deal (Bloomberg/WSJ, mid-July). Negotiations remain at an impasse on structural issues — IP protection, forced tech transfer, and enforcement mechanisms.

The action stance of negotiate (slightly below neutral at -0.1) reflects: (1) the domestic economy needs stability and time to absorb stimulus measures already deployed (2T yuan in tax cuts, 6 RRR cuts); (2) the Huawei situation creates genuine tech vulnerability that needs time to mitigate through domestic substitution; (3) but making concessions under pressure — particularly large agricultural purchase commitments without tariff rollback — would weaken China's negotiating position and embolden further US demands. The correct play is to engage seriously in talks, signal willingness to increase purchases if tariffs are rolled back, and preserve retaliatory tools as deterrents rather than deploying them.
key_factors: GDP growth at 27-year low (6.2% Q2 2019) — trade war clearly biting
Huawei Entity List threatens tech self-sufficiency goals; 1,200+ supplier firms affected
US threatens additional tariffs on ~$300B of remaining Chinese imports
China controls 90%+ of rare earths — significant leverage not yet deployed
Unreliable entity list announced but not yet populated — credible deterrent
G20 truce fragile; agricultural purchase dispute reveals trust deficit
Factory employment declining at fastest pace since 2008 crisis
Beijing stimulus deployed (2T yuan tax cuts, 6 RRR cuts) but economy slow to respond
US also faces costs: UBS estimates 1pp GDP hit from full China tariffs, Fed signaling rate cuts

sources_cited.excerpt: US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi.
China announces it will establish an 'unreliable entity list' targeting foreign firms that cut supplies to Chinese companies for non-commercial reasons.
G20 Osaka: Trump and Xi agree to resume talks. Existing tariffs remain; no new tariffs 'for the time being.'
China's economic growth has slumped to its lowest level in nearly three decades... grew at 6.2% in the quarter ended June, the slowest quarterly growth rate since 1992.

China accounts for more than 90 per cent of rare earths exports... 'The Chinese people would never agree to the US using products made from rare earths exported from China to curb and suppress China's development.'
China has made no official mention of a commitment to purchasing more U.S. agricultural products... no unusually large purchases have been reported since then.
